content_preview.title: Veracode's Fall 2026 Report Finds AI Code Security Gains Concentrated in Easy Fixes as Developer Trust Climbs
content_preview.summary: Veracode's Fall 2026 benchmark shows AI models' first meaningful security gain in a year, concentrated in easy fixes, as a separate Stack Overflow survey finds developer trust in AI output has far outpaced that caution.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

AI models produced more secure code in the third quarter of 2026 than they had in over a year, according to [Veracode](https://www.veracode.com/blog/fall-2026-genai-code-security/), whose Fall 2026 GenAI Code Security Report found the average security pass rate across 18 tested models rose from 56% to 62% and the vulnerability rate fell from roughly 44% to roughly 38%. editor_notes.content_quality: Well-structured Analysis with a clear Overview/Background/Current situation/Implications arc. Facts are cleanly separated from analysis: the first three sections report Veracode's and Stack Overflow's figures with attribution, and the 'Implications' section is explicitly framed as the Herald's own reading ('Read together...', 'Whether that gap ... narrows depends on information that neither data set currently provides'), never presenting the comparison itself as a vendor- or survey-confirmed fact. 1267 words, within the 800-2000 Analysis band. Tone is neutral and analytical throughout, no sensationalism, no AI self-reference.

Independent-source count for the Analysis requirement: 2 of 4 (TechRadar and Stack Overflow are independent of Veracode, the subject of the primary benchmark story; the two Veracode URLs are the vendor's own posts) -- meets the >=2-independent threshold. Allowlist: added veracode.com and survey.stackoverflow.co to config/source_allowlist.txt in this review's commit, each confirmed as the organization's own official site (masthead/footer/byline checked against the snapshot) per the policy's confirmation procedure; techradar.com was already allowlisted. Anthropic disclosure: not required - Claude Opus 5.5/Claude Sonnet 5.5 appear only as two of 18 benchmarked models in a leaderboard, not as the subject of the headline/summary/lead, and there is no 'assisted by Claude' credit line.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Found two subordinate derived-figure errors, both outside the headline/summary/lead: (1) 'Background' section states the Java-to-next-language gap is '26 percentage points below the next-lowest language, C#' -- the source's own 26-point figure (Java 31.00% vs. the figure immediately above it) is the gap to JavaScript (56.99%; 56.99-31.00=25.99=26pts), not C# (59.55%; a 28.55-point gap). The article misnames which language the 26-point figure is measured against. (2) 'Current situation' section states the large/medium/small model-size pass-rate spread (55%/52%/51%=4pts) 'has grown from one percentage point to four since October 2025.' The source does give a 4-point current spread for model size, but the '1 percentage point' starting value and its growth trajectory belong to a different comparison in the same Veracode post -- general-purpose vs. coding-specialized models (54% vs 51%=3pts, up from 'about 1 percentage point' in July 2026, not October 2025). The source's own language for the size comparison going back to October 2025 is that model size then had 'essentially no effect,' not a quantified 1-point gap. The article conflates two distinct comparisons from the source into one incorrect combined claim. Both errors are subordinate (Background and Current-situation body paragraphs, not the headline, summary, or Overview lead) and each is a single, nameable mislabeling that a corrections note can honestly and completely resolve without gutting the article's thesis. Every other specific number, quote, and attribution checked against raw source text verified exactly (see source_verification) -- this is not a pattern of fabrication, it is two related but distinct derived-figure slips in a piece that otherwise handles a large volume of statistics correctly.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and analytical. No loaded language, no editorializing beyond the explicitly-flagged Implications section, no promotional framing of either Veracode's product or Stack Overflow.
editor_notes.originality: No prior Herald coverage of Veracode or of the 2026 Stack Overflow Developer Survey found (checked via grep across src/content/articles/ and the 2026-11 folder). Related but distinct prior coverage exists: 2026-08/31-contrast-security-report-finds-ai-application-security-scanners-agree-on-just-5-of-findings (AI AppSec tooling gaps) and 2026-11/26-ai-coding-tools-boost-code-output-but-three-2026-studies-find-review-and-debugging-became-the-new-bottleneck (AI coding tool quality/review burden studies), both added as related_articles in the article-meta file. This is a new topic and angle, not a duplicate.
concerns: Two subordinate derived-figure errors in the Background and Current-situation sections (the Java/C# vs Java/JavaScript gap figure, and the model-size spread's claimed growth trajectory and timeframe) -- addressed via corrections record, not grounds for rejection since neither touches the headline/summary/lead and both are independently and honestly correctable.
recommendations: File a corrections record with two entries covering the Java-language-gap misattribution and the model-size-spread conflation.

Writer should double check which specific comparison (and which baseline year) a given percentage-point figure belongs to when a single source article runs multiple similar model-cohort comparisons side by side.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: A solid Analysis that meets the format requirements (1267 words, 4 sources with 2 independent of Veracode, genuine cross-source comparison rather than a single-release recap, facts and analysis clearly separated) and whose major claims -- the 56%->62% pass-rate jump, the CWE-level breakdown, the Java-language gap's existence, and the Stack Overflow trust figures -- all verify verbatim against the raw snapshots. Two subordinate derived-figure errors (a mislabeled comparison language and a conflated model-size growth figure) keep this from a clean APPROVE but are each independently correctable in a short corrections note without touching the headline, summary, or lead. Featured candidacy: 1 - solid, well-sourced analysis for a developer/AppSec audience of a routine quarterly benchmark update, not an industry-wide inflection point.
